opening.headline: When a coding agent attempts to execute dangerous commands, where and how can we block it?
body: The coding agent deletes files, executes commands, and uploads code to a repository. It is common to enable automatic approval mode so that humans do not have to monitor every action, but dangerous commands are immediately executed when proposed.

In this lesson, we examine two points at which safeguards can be implemented using Claude Code as an example. One is a declarative rule involving permission modes and allow/confirm/reject rules, and the other is a check known as the PreToolUse hook that intervenes just before tool execution. We read the configuration file line by line and establish criteria to determine which risks should be assigned to which side.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of privilege mode and the hook before execution
You can distinguish between risks posed by hooks and risks posed by permission rules.

screens.title: I want to block before the risky command is executed
screens.lead: This scene shows a coding agent suggesting a dangerous command while performing cleanup tasks. Please read it carefully, considering where the obstruction might be placed.

visual.alt: A diagram showing how two defensive measures meet at a stop line just before the command proposed by the agent is executed.

paragraphs: The coding agent is attempting to execute a bulk delete command while organizing the build folder. The system is currently running in automatic approval mode because a person cannot monitor the screen continuously. The command has already been proposed and cannot be undone at the moment of execution.

In this scenario, there are two places where blocking can occur. First, there are permission rules. These rules declare in advance that one command is always blocked, while another always requires confirmation. Second, there is a hook. Before the tool executes, a script defined by the user is inserted, which checks the command's content and decides whether to block it.

Although these two methods appear similar, they serve different purposes. The question of this lesson is: which risks should be declared as rules and which risks should be checked via hooks. Before we proceed, let's first consider what we are checking when using the auto-approval mode.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: A hook is a user-defined procedure that runs automatically at a predefined point in the lifecycle. It can be a shell command, an HTTP endpoint, or an MCP tool call.

screens.outro: First, let's recall the inspection items when using the automatic approval mode.

screens.title: When using auto-approval mode, recall what is being verified.
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please try answering it yourself before clicking.

items.prompt: Do you fully understand the scope of tasks that are automatically approved?
items.answer: The scope of automatic execution varies depending on the mode. There are modes that automatically perform only reading, modes that automatically perform file editing, and modes that are nearly fully automatic. Do not assume based solely on the mode name—always verify the scope first.

items.prompt: Have you defined actions that must always be blocked, regardless of user approval?
items.answer: At the moment automatic approval is enabled, human verification is removed, so actions that must never be executed under any circumstances should be predefined. Examples include bulk deletion or reading of confidential files. It is safer to fix such actions via declaration.

items.prompt: Can we enable the auto-approval mode in my unisolated work environment?
items.answer: The wider the automatic approval, the greater the risk of errors spreading to your files and accounts. The most permissive mode is recommended only for use within isolated containers or virtual machines. When setting the mode, also consider the level of isolation in the execution environment alongside convenience.

screens.outro: Let's continue our comparison by examining how the automatic approval scope varies across different modes.

screens.title: Scope of execution without prompting by permission mode
screens.lead: Compare the scope and appropriate use cases for each tab, without being prompted about permissions in different mode settings.

tabs.label: default
tabs.body: In basic mode, execution occurs without prompting and consists solely of reading. This mode is also referred to as manual and represents the most conservative baseline. File modifications or command executions require confirmation. It is appropriate when performing sensitive operations or when you wish to review all actions directly.

tabs.label: acceptEdits
tabs.body: In addition to reading, it automatically approves common file operations such as file editing and commands like `mkdir`, `mv`, and `cp`. When you want to continue verifying actions other than editing—such as when repeatedly modifying reviewed code—editing can be delegated, but other actions must still be confirmed.

tabs.label: plan
tabs.body: This is a mode focused on reading, allowing you to first explore the codebase. It is appropriate to use this before making changes, when you need to understand the structure and plan your approach. Similar to when you first open a unfamiliar repository, it helps prevent accidental modifications to files when you haven't yet decided what specifically to change.

tabs.label: auto
tabs.body: A separate classification model reviews each action in place of a human, blocking actions deemed risky. Since this mode replaces human verification with model review, it is important to understand and use the actions that are blocked.

tabs.label: bypassPermissions
tabs.body: Almost all operations are automatically executed. This mode is intended to be used only within isolated containers or virtual machines. Denial rules still apply in this mode, so any actions that need to be blocked should be explicitly declared in rules.

screens.outro: The mode is merely the starting point, so we will now read the rules for allowance, confirmation, and rejection that are layered upon it from the configuration file.

screens.title: Allow/Confirm/Reject Rules: Read the configuration file line by line
screens.lead: The following is an example of permission settings. By selecting a line range from the right-side description, you can view both the behavior determined by that line and the symptoms that appear when it is incorrectly configured.

notes.note: Rules are defined under `permissions`. Allow rules are executed without inquiry, ask rules always require a question, and deny rules block execution. The evaluation order is deny, then ask, then allow, with the first matching rule determining the outcome. It is easy to mistakenly believe that allow wins when the same command is specified both as allow and ask, if one does not understand this structure.

`defaultMode` is the baseline authorization mode. If set to `acceptEdits`, file editing and common file operations are automatically approved. If this value is set to a broader mode than intended, operations that normally require confirmation will be executed silently.

`Bash(npm run build)` executes this command without querying; since there is no asterisk, it only matches commands that are exactly identical, and does not allow commands with different arguments. An asterisk should be added only when necessary, as it broadens the scope.

`Bash(git push *)` always prompts the user regardless of mode when a command begins with `git push`. This serves the purpose of recording human confirmation when exposing code externally. Without this rule, a push could be executed without confirmation in automatic approval mode.

`deny`'s `Bash(rm *)` and `Read(./.env)` block delete commands and `.env` read operations in all modes including `bypassPermissions`. If a prohibited command is incorrectly specified in allow, it will continue to execute, and paths outside the working directory require separate rules.

screens.outro: The rule is simple as a declaration but cannot assess situations. Let's see when the hook responsible for this role is executed.

screens.title: The moment when hook is executed
screens.lead: When you select the image number marker, you can view the timing and usage of the associated event. Find out where you can block a call.

visual.alt: A horizontal timeline showing hook events from session start through before and after tool calls.

markers.label: SessionStart
markers.title: When a session starts or is re-established
markers.body: Occurs when starting or resuming a session. Can be used for preparing the work environment or recording the current state. Not suitable for preventing tool calls.

markers.label: UserPromptSubmit
markers.title: Immediately after sending the prompt
markers.body: This occurs immediately after the user sends a prompt, before Claude processes it. It can be used for input validation or logging. Since no tool calls have been created yet, it is not suitable for blocking at the command level.

markers.label: PreToolUse
markers.title: Before the tool call is executed
markers.body: This occurs just before tool execution and can block the call. The handler receives event information in JSON format, inspects the command, arguments, and path, and returns a decision. Dangerous command blocking is performed here.

markers.label: PermissionRequest
markers.title: When permission determination is required
markers.body: Occurs at the time a permission decision is needed. Can be used to verify or log the situation before prompting the user.

markers.label: PostToolUse
markers.title: After the tool call is successful
markers.body: Occurs after a tool call succeeds. Since it has already been executed, it cannot prevent the call, but is used to record results or continue with subsequent actions. This event occurs identically across terminals, IDEs, desktop applications, and cloud sessions.

screens.outro: Since we've confirmed that the blockable point is PreToolUse, let's now examine the hook configuration on a line-by-line basis.

screens.title: Read preToolUse hook settings on a per-line basis
screens.lead: The following is a hook configuration for checking the deletion command of Bash tools. Review the per-line explanations to verify each field's role and observe symptoms when discrepancies occur.

notes.note: `PreToolUse` declares a reaction prior to tool invocation, while `matcher` is a tool name filter. Since its value is `Bash`, it only responds to Bash tool invocations. If the matcher does not match another tool name, the hook will not execute at all, and the delete command will pass through unchanged.

`type` indicates that this handler is a shell command. `if` represents additional conditions of the grammar, such as permission rules, and the script executes only when a subordinate command begins with `rm`. Thanks to this condition, the script does not need to run every time a Bash command is invoked.

`command` is the path to the script to be executed. `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` points to the project folder. If the script file is missing or lacks execution permissions, the check itself will not run. Therefore, after setting up the configuration, you must also verify the execution permissions.

screens.outro: Having learned how to read configurations, let us now move on to an example where the instructor deliberately corrects a wrongly written configuration.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Fixing a hook that passed through a delete command
screens.lead: There is a case where the PreToolUse hook has been installed, yet the agent's deletion command is not blocked. Select the arrow to proceed step by step through the instructor's diagnostic process.

steps.title: Check for symptoms
steps.body: The agent's `rm -rf` command was executed as-is, even though a hook was installed. The settings were configured to paths `"matcher": "Write"`, `"if": "Bash(rm *)"`, and `block-rm.sh`.

steps.title: First, we check whether the hook has moved.
steps.body: Before checking if the validation criteria are weak, first verify whether the hook was executed at all. In this configuration, since the matcher is `Write`, the hook was not executed during the Bash call. The script itself had no issues.

steps.title: Fix the matcher
steps.body:
Replace the matcher with `"Bash"`. Then, the script will only execute when the command starts with `rm`, in conjunction with the `if` condition. The script extracts the command from JSON input via standard input, checks it for risks, and returns `deny` if it detects any risk.

```
#!/bin/bash
# .claude/hooks/block-rm.sh
COMMAND=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command')

if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then
  jq -n '{
    hookSpecificOutput: {
      hookEventName: "PreToolUse",
      permissionDecision: "deny",
      permissionDecisionReason: "Destructive command blocked by hook"
    }
  }'
else
  exit 0
fi
```

steps.title: Points left unaddressed are highlighted.
steps.body: This script checks only for the string `rm -rf`. Other forms of deletion commands may pass. If considered safe, the script ends with `exit 0` without making a decision, allowing the existing permission flow to continue. If a command must always be blocked, declaring a `deny` rule such as `Bash(rm *)` is simpler.

steps.title: Verify the results
steps.body: When blocked, Claude Code informs the model of the rejection without executing the tool. The model then seeks an alternative approach. A silent hook does not indicate approval but rather the absence of a decision; thus, passed calls proceed to receive judgment from the authorization rules and mode.

screens.outro: Having fixed the configuration errors, I'll now clarify the criteria for determining whether to assign risks to rules or to hooks.

screens.title: Rules to block and hooks to block
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the local rules, hooks, and the inspection location and scope of inference hooks.

states.label: Local rules and hook
states.body: Rules are declarations that always reject specific tools or command patterns. They are simple and consistently applied across all modes. In contrast, checks that require examining command arguments, paths, or content, as well as logging and notifications, are handled by hooks. Conditions involving checks not expressible through rules fall under the responsibility of hooks. Both rules and hooks are installed and managed via configuration files, so their installation status may vary depending on the user's environment.

states.label: Inference hook
states.body: The organization's server responds with either `allow` or `deny` before executing any prompts or tool calls. This check occurs within the Claude infrastructure and does not depend on any locally installed software on employee devices. It is used for controls that need to be consistently applied across the entire organization, such as data leakage prevention, audit logging, and policy enforcement. Unlike local hooks, it is difficult for individual users to circumvent by modifying local settings.

screens.outro: Each component has been assigned its role; now I will summarize the previous content into a single cohesive point.

screens.title: Unified summary: Rules are declarations, hooks are checks
screens.lead: Go back to the first question and summarize. Look at the flow to identify where the risk command is blocked.

paragraphs: The means to block dangerous commands consist of two layers. The permission mode serves as a baseline that defines the scope within which actions can be executed, upon which top-level rules for allowance, confirmation, and denial are superimposed. Rules are evaluated in the order of denial, confirmation, and allowance, and denial rules apply across all modes including those containing `bypassPermissions`. Therefore, actions that must always be blocked should be declared using denial rules.

If a rule is declared, then a hook is a check. The `PreToolUse` hook is invoked just before tool execution and examines the command arguments and path to decide whether to block. However, if `matcher` and `if` do not match the actual invocation, the hook will not execute at all, and silence should be remembered as not being approval but rather absence of decision.

If the same policy needs to be applied across the entire organization, there is an approach similar to a reasoning hook that performs checks before execution on the server. Ultimately, whether and where a risk is mitigated depends on whether the risk is a simple pattern or requires contextual judgment, as well as who is responsible for managing the policies.

checks.intro: Apply the evaluation order of the configuration file you just read. Results are not recorded.
checks.q:
What happens if we run "git push origin main" under the following settings?  
"allow": ["Bash(git push *)"], "ask": ["Bash(git push *)"]
options: allow is evaluated first and is ignored
Session fails to start due to configuration error
checks.explain: Rules are evaluated in the order of rejection, confirmation, and allowance, and the first matching rule determines the outcome. If the same command exists in ask, it always prompts the user.

wrong.0: Even if "allow" is present, "ask" is evaluated first, so execution does not occur without being queried.
wrong.2: The evaluation order is rejection, confirmation, allowance.
wrong.3: The same pattern may exist in both lists without indicating a configuration error.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. When the same pattern exists in two lists, the verification rule is evaluated before the allow rule.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Review the evaluation order again. Since the allowed rules are evaluated last, this option is incorrect.

checks.intro: Whenever you're considering blocking, pair the appropriate measures and check them against your own standards. Scores are not saved.
checks.q: Pair up the situation of attempting to restrict with the appropriate means.
left: Always reject a specific tool in any mode
Assess risk based on command arguments and paths
Check before executing all tool calls from the organizational server
Record the results after the tool succeeds
checks.explain: Simple and consistent blocking is handled by declarative rules, while the situation assessment is managed by the PreToolUse hook. The inference hook operates by having the organization server respond with allow or deny prior to execution, and logging after success occurs at the PostToolUse stage.
checks.correctFeedback: Both pairs are correct. The test cases are well divided, with sufficient blocking and situational judgment provided through declarations.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The pair is slightly misaligned. Please re-connect them based on whether the call is made before or after execution, and whether it's a declaration or a check.

glossary.def: This sets the boundary defining the range of actions executed without being explicitly requested in a session.
Permission rules that declare whether execution occurs based on tool and command patterns. Evaluated in the order: deny, confirm, allow.
A hook event that operates just before a tool call is executed and can prevent the call from proceeding.
A feature that allows an organization's server to inspect all prompts and tool calls before execution, and respond with either allow or deny.
This is a configuration field that filters the tool name that the hook will respond to.

misconceptions.myth: In bypassPermissions mode, everything is allowed.
misconceptions.fact: Rejection rules apply in this mode as well. Therefore, actions that need to be blocked in any mode should be declared using rejection rules.

misconceptions.myth: As long as you write the rules correctly, hooks are unnecessary.
misconceptions.fact: Rules declare patterns; it is difficult to express checks that evaluate command content. Such checks, logging, and notifications are handled by hooks.

misconceptions.myth: The hook's matcher applies to any tool.
misconceptions.fact: matcher is a tool name filter. To block Bash commands, it must match the Bash invocation; otherwise, the hook will not be executed at all.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Rules are declarations and hooks are checks.
The permission mode is the baseline, and rules are overlaid and applied upon it.
The rejection rule applies in all modes.
PreToolUse is a blocking point just before execution, and it must be matched and called in sync with the if statement to execute.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are intended for you to think about on your own and are not submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: In our environment, at what point do we actually prevent dangerous actions—through rules, through hooks, or are we still missing something?
